evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a peer-reviewed, Pfizer/Valneva-funded prospective study (BOLD) that tracked 797 medically attended Lyme borreliosis (Lyme disease) cases at 14 primary-care practices in six European countries between April 2021 and December 2022. It reports how often patients had the classic erythema migrans rash versus disseminated disease (such as Lyme arthritis, neuroborreliosis, or carditis), how long it took from symptom onset to diagnosis, how often patients were hospitalized, what antibiotics were prescribed and for how long, and how common prior tick bites or prior Lyme episodes were among enrolled patients. The study found striking country-to-country variation, especially in Slovakia, where 76% of cases were Lyme arthritis compared to about 3.5% elsewhere, a pattern the authors say could reflect several possible, not-yet-distinguishable causes. The document does not report any dollar costs, income loss, caregiving burden, or insurance/access-barrier data; it is a clinical-manifestations and treatment-pattern study, not an economic cost-of-illness analysis.

spec.title: Lyme Disease Diagnostic Delay, Country-Level Manifestation Variation, and Antibiotic Treatment Patterns (BOLD Study)
spec.boundary: This simulation covers only non-monetary, time- and percentage-based findings from the prospective BOLD study of 797 medically attended Lyme borreliosis cases (315 enrolled with detailed data) across six European countries, 2021-2022: diagnostic delay by manifestation type, country-level variation in Lyme-arthritis share, antibiotic treatment duration, and prior-episode history. It omits all dollar costs, income loss, caregiving time, insurance/access barriers, PTLDS burden (explicitly deferred by the authors to a separate manuscript), and quantified adverse-event rates, because this document reports none of these. The reported sex differences in manifestation type (more females with erythema migrans, more males with disseminated disease) are not modeled as sliders here but are preserved in the documentation.

takeaway.patient: In this study, patients whose Lyme disease showed up as the classic rash were diagnosed faster on average (about 13 days from symptom start) than patients with disseminated disease such as Lyme arthritis, neurological symptoms, or heart involvement (about 25 days), or patients with less typical presentations (about 39 days, though based on only 12 people). About a third of enrolled patients had had Lyme disease before. Most people who needed antibiotics were treated for roughly two weeks, but a few needed much longer courses (up to 93 days in this study).
takeaway.care: BOLD's enrolled-cohort data show disseminated and atypical presentations took roughly 1.5-3x longer to reach diagnosis than classic erythema migrans, suggesting a lower index of suspicion or more complex workup for non-rash presentations. Slovakia's markedly higher Lyme-arthritis share (76.3% vs ~3.5% elsewhere) coincided with relatively more one-tier serologic testing there, though the authors cannot separate this from other contributing factors (co-infection, healthcare-seeking behavior, rural setting, case classification). Antibiotic course length varied widely, including a few multi-month courses.
takeaway.policy: BOLD documents large cross-country variation in Lyme-arthritis share and in time-to-diagnosis by manifestation, against a backdrop of historically inconsistent European LB surveillance and testing practices that the study itself was designed to standardize. No cost data exist in this document, so any economic framing must stay limited to time/utilization metrics, not translated into expenditure.

patient: If your symptoms include joint swelling, neurological changes, or heart-related symptoms rather than (or in addition to) a rash, ask your clinician how that might affect how quickly Lyme disease gets recognized, since this study found such presentations took noticeably longer to diagnose than the classic rash.
If you have had Lyme disease before, mention that history clearly when you seek care, since about a third of patients in this study had a prior episode.

If you are prescribed antibiotics for much longer than two to three weeks, ask what is driving that specific recommendation and what to expect, since most people in this study were treated for a shorter period.
care: Review whether disseminated or atypical presentations in your own setting are being recognized as quickly as classic erythema migrans, benchmarking against this cohort's roughly 25- and 39-day average delays versus 13 days for EM.

This finding may be worth checking against your own testing pathway (one-tier vs two-tier serology) and case-definition practices, given BOLD's observation (which it cannot fully explain) that higher one-tier test use coincided with a much higher Lyme-arthritis share in one country.
Flag antibiotic courses markedly longer than the ~2-3 week typical range for case review, since a small number of BOLD cases required 48-93 day courses.
Document prior-LB-episode history systematically at intake, since over a third of enrolled cases reported a previous episode.
policy: Use the country-level Lyme-arthritis share difference to prioritize further investigation (testing-practice audits, subspecies/co-infection studies, care-seeking research) rather than to conclude overdiagnosis or underdiagnosis in any one country, since the study's authors identify several possible, unranked contributing causes.

Support continued harmonization of serologic testing approaches and case definitions across surveillance systems, consistent with BOLD's own stated motivation for a standardized, multi-country surveillance approach.

Compare observed antibiotic-duration patterns against each country's own guideline-recommended durations to see where real-world prescribing diverges from guidance, while noting this document provides no cost data to translate duration into expenditure.

When using these diagnostic-delay or manifestation figures for planning, account for the document's own finding that enrolled and unenrolled cases differ systematically (more disseminated disease, older age, more female among enrolled).

package.documentation:
**Source & scope:** All figures come from the BOLD study (peer-reviewed, Pfizer/Valneva-funded), a prospective cohort of 797 medically attended Lyme borreliosis (LB) cases at 14 primary-care practices in six European countries, April 2021-December 2022; detailed symptom/treatment-timing statistics are reported only for a 315-case enrolled subset. This document contains no dollar costs, income-loss, caregiving-time, or insurance/access-barrier data - every number here is a day-count, percentage, or rate, not a monetary estimate.

**Diagnostic delay** inputs (mean days from symptom onset to diagnosis: 13.4 EM, 24.9 disseminated, 38.5 'other'/unclassified, n=12 for the last) are the document's own pooled enrolled-cohort means (p.8); the 'other' figure rests on a very small sample. The two delay-gap outputs subtract these to show how much slower disseminated or atypical presentations were recognized relative to EM in this cohort.

**Country-level Lyme-arthritis (LA) share**: Slovakia's LA share (76.3% of its 173 cases) is compared against roughly 3.5% in the other five countries. The authors state this large gap could reflect several unranked, not-separable causes - Borrelia subspecies/co-infection differences, healthcare-seeking behavior, diagnostic/serologic testing practices (Slovakia used relatively more one-tier testing), COVID-19-related delay, rural setting, or differential case classification. The difference output is an illustrative arithmetic comparison only; it does not measure or test any single cause, and input ranges are deliberately narrowed (Slovakia 50-90%, others 0-20%) so sliders cannot flip this documented ordering.

**Antibiotic duration** (mean 15 days, median 11, range 2-93 across 302 cases) and the **previous-episode share** (35.6% of 315 enrolled cases reported a prior LB episode) are reported as single pooled cohort figures.

**Limitations:**
- Subgroup disaggregation: The pooled diagnostic-delay, hospitalization (1.3%), and previous-episode figures are not broken down by sex, age, or race/ethnicity, even though the document itself reports sex differences (more females presented with EM: 80.7% vs 73.1% males; more males with disseminated disease: 26.9% vs 19.3%). Federal survey data (MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) generally supports disaggregated analysis even where this document did not perform one.
- Systemic evidence gap: Before BOLD, European LB surveillance relied on inconsistent diagnostic/testing practices (one-tier vs two-tier serology) and no unified case definitions, limiting comparability across countries - a limitation of the surveillance system itself, separate from the accuracy or funding of any single estimate here.
- Enrolled (n=315) and unenrolled (n=482) cases differ systematically (more disseminated disease, older, more female among enrolled), so delay/treatment statistics should not be generalized to all 797 cases.
- No cost, PTLDS, or adverse-event-rate data exist in this document; PTLDS findings are explicitly deferred to a separate manuscript.

spec.title: Lyme Disease Diagnostic Delay, Country-Level Manifestation Variation, and Antibiotic Treatment Patterns (BOLD Study)
spec.boundary: This simulation covers only non-monetary, time- and percentage-based findings from the prospective BOLD study of 797 medically attended Lyme borreliosis cases (315 enrolled with detailed data) across six European countries, 2021-2022: diagnostic delay by manifestation type, country-level variation in Lyme-arthritis share, antibiotic treatment duration, and prior-episode history. It omits all dollar costs, income loss, caregiving time, insurance/access barriers, PTLDS burden (explicitly deferred by the authors to a separate manuscript), and quantified adverse-event rates, because this document reports none of these. The reported sex differences in manifestation type (more females with erythema migrans, more males with disseminated disease) are not modeled as sliders here but are preserved in the documentation.

takeaway.patient: In this study, patients whose Lyme disease showed up as the classic rash were diagnosed faster on average (about 13 days from symptom start) than patients with disseminated disease such as Lyme arthritis, neurological symptoms, or heart involvement (about 25 days), or patients with less typical presentations (about 39 days, though based on only 12 people). About a third of enrolled patients had had Lyme disease before. Most people who needed antibiotics were treated for roughly two weeks, but a few needed much longer courses (up to 93 days in this study).
takeaway.care: BOLD's enrolled-cohort data show disseminated and atypical presentations took roughly 1.5-3x longer to reach diagnosis than classic erythema migrans, suggesting a lower index of suspicion or more complex workup for non-rash presentations. Slovakia's markedly higher Lyme-arthritis share (76.3% vs ~3.5% elsewhere) coincided with relatively more one-tier serologic testing there, though the authors cannot separate this from other contributing factors (co-infection, healthcare-seeking behavior, rural setting, case classification). Antibiotic course length varied widely, including a few multi-month courses.
takeaway.policy: BOLD documents large cross-country variation in Lyme-arthritis share and in time-to-diagnosis by manifestation, against a backdrop of historically inconsistent European LB surveillance and testing practices that the study itself was designed to standardize. No cost data exist in this document, so any economic framing must stay limited to time/utilization metrics, not translated into expenditure.

patient: If your symptoms include joint swelling, neurological changes, or heart-related symptoms rather than (or in addition to) a rash, ask your clinician how that might affect how quickly Lyme disease gets recognized, since this study found such presentations took noticeably longer to diagnose than the classic rash.
If you have had Lyme disease before, mention that history clearly when you seek care, since about a third of patients in this study had a prior episode.

If you are prescribed antibiotics for much longer than two to three weeks, ask what is driving that specific recommendation and what to expect, since most people in this study were treated for a shorter period.
care: Review whether disseminated or atypical presentations in your own setting are being recognized as quickly as classic erythema migrans, benchmarking against this cohort's roughly 25- and 39-day average delays versus 13 days for EM.

This finding may be worth checking against your own testing pathway (one-tier vs two-tier serology) and case-definition practices, given BOLD's observation (which it cannot fully explain) that higher one-tier test use coincided with a much higher Lyme-arthritis share in one country.
Flag antibiotic courses markedly longer than the ~2-3 week typical range for case review, since a small number of BOLD cases required 48-93 day courses.
Document prior-LB-episode history systematically at intake, since over a third of enrolled cases reported a previous episode.
policy: Use the country-level Lyme-arthritis share difference to prioritize further investigation (testing-practice audits, subspecies/co-infection studies, care-seeking research) rather than to conclude overdiagnosis or underdiagnosis in any one country, since the study's authors identify several possible, unranked contributing causes.

Support continued harmonization of serologic testing approaches and case definitions across surveillance systems, consistent with BOLD's own stated motivation for a standardized, multi-country surveillance approach.

Compare observed antibiotic-duration patterns against each country's own guideline-recommended durations to see where real-world prescribing diverges from guidance, while noting this document provides no cost data to translate duration into expenditure.

When using these diagnostic-delay or manifestation figures for planning, account for the document's own finding that enrolled and unenrolled cases differ systematically (more disseminated disease, older age, more female among enrolled).
